analysis.one_liner: Cuts soda ash royalties on federal land for five years and creates ten national heritage areas.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared both chambers with overwhelming bipartisan support — 323-39 in the House, unanimous consent twice in the Senate — and became Public Law 109-338 on October 12, 2006, cutting soda ash royalties to 2% for five years while designating ten national heritage areas.
analysis.plain_summary: This law does two very different things. It cuts the royalty companies pay to mine sodium compounds (soda ash) from federal land to 2% for five years, which mainly helps a concentrated Wyoming mining industry at a cost to the federal treasury and royalty-sharing states. It also creates ten National Heritage Areas — including the Gullah/Geechee corridor honoring African-American coastal history — giving local nonprofits federal recognition and matching grants to preserve and promote historic and cultural sites, with no federal money for land acquisition.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and local organizations in ten regions get federal heritage recognition, tourism promotion, and matching grants (capped at $1 million per area per year, with a 50% local match) for preserving historic sites and cultural traditions. Soda ash producers get a five-year reduction in the royalty they owe on federal-land minerals. Local water agencies, notably the Santa Clara Valley Water District, gain access to a new federal groundwater cleanup fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heritage-area communities and soda ash producers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes ten National Heritage Areas with federal technical and financial assistance to conserve, interpret, and promote natural, historic, and cultural resources — for example, the Gullah/Geechee corridor recognizes and helps preserve the culture of African-American communities along the South Atlantic coast.

Each heritage area is authorized up to $10 million (no more than $1 million per year) with a federal share capped at 50 percent, so federal dollars leverage local matching funds for preservation, interpretive exhibits, and heritage tourism.

Includes extensive private-property protections: local entities may not use federal funds to acquire land, property cannot be listed or promoted without the owner's written consent, and owners can have their property removed from an area's boundary by written request.

Lowers the royalty rate on sodium compounds produced from federal land to 2 percent for five years, reducing costs for producers, and directs Interior to report after four years on production and jobs created or maintained.

Authorizes feasibility studies for additional heritage areas (Western Reserve, St. Croix, Southern Campaign of the Revolution, Delaware coast), reauthorizes the Blackstone River Valley Corridor, and creates a federal fund for groundwater cleanup in California's Santa Clara Valley.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. treasury takes in less from soda ash royalties for five years, and the states that share those royalties — Wyoming above all — lose their portion of that revenue. Taxpayers fund the heritage-area grants and studies, though every area requires 50 percent local matching funds and each authorization sunsets after 15 years.

drawbacks.text: The soda ash royalty cut transfers revenue from federal land to a single mining industry for five years, and the bill directs Interior to study whether the reduced rate should continue afterward — building a case for making the giveaway permanent.

The package bundles many unrelated items — a Wyoming royalty cut, a California water storage study, a Delaware coastal study, a groundwater fund, and West Virginia coal-heritage amendments — so one popular conservation vehicle carried provisions that would likely not have passed scrutiny on their own.

Heritage-area designations cover entire counties, and critics worry federal designations can bring outside planning pressure; the bill tries to answer this with owner-consent, withdrawal, and no-land-acquisition rules, but those safeguards depend on local entities following them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The heritage-area designations deliver modest but real public benefits: locally matched money for preserving historic sites, cultural recognition for communities like the Gullah/Geechee, and heritage tourism, all wrapped in strong private-property safeguards and 15-year sunsets. The cost is a five-year royalty giveaway to soda ash producers on federal land, worth tens of millions in foregone federal and state revenue, attached to a study designed to justify extending it. The public gains are genuine but small in dollar terms; the industry benefit is the least defensible part of an otherwise popular package.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it — the Senate twice by unanimous consent and the House 323-39 on a fast-track suspension vote — and President Bush signed it into law as Public Law 109-338 on October 12, 2006.

narrative.text: Sen. Craig Thomas (R-WY) introduced the bill on January 31, 2005, originally as the Soda Ash Royalty Reduction Act of 2005, cutting the federal sodium-compounds royalty to 2 percent for five years.

The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, chaired by Sen. Pete Domenici, reported the bill favorably without amendment just over two weeks after introduction, and it was placed on the Senate calendar on February 16, 2005.

The Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent on July 26, 2005, by then expanded into the National Heritage Areas Act with ten heritage areas, three studies, and other public-lands items added as titles.

The bill sat in two House subcommittees for nearly a year before Rep. Greg Walden brought it to the floor under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority — on July 24, 2006; it passed 323-39, with every voting Democrat in favor and 39 Republicans opposed.
The Senate agreed to the House amendment by unanimous consent on September 29, 2006, and President Bush signed the bill on October 12, 2006, making it Public Law 109-338.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wyoming soda ash producers gained a five-year royalty cut, and ten regional heritage nonprofits and their communities gained federal recognition and up to $1 million a year each in matching preservation funds. The 39 House Republicans who voted no came out behind on the record: their objections never slowed a package both chambers' leadership moved quickly.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Soda ash producers and heritage-area nonprofits

for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably without amendment two weeks after introduction and managed its Senate passage.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelming in both parties: the Senate passed it twice by unanimous consent, and the House vote of 323-39 included 163 Democrats (zero opposed) and 159 Republicans — every one of the 39 no votes came from Republicans.

industries.note: The bill sets the royalty on sodium compounds produced from federal land at 2 percent for five years, overriding the standard Mineral Leasing Act rate — a direct revenue transfer from the treasury and royalty-sharing states (Wyoming above all) to producers. The bill's four-year study of jobs and royalties builds the record for extending the cut.

industries.industry: Heritage tourism and local preservation nonprofits
industries.note: The law names ten specific nonprofits and commissions as the local coordinating entities for their heritage areas, making them the channel for up to $1 million a year each in federal matching funds for 15 years. Their interest runs with the communities they serve, though it permanently places federal heritage funding in private hands.

industries.industry: California water agencies (Santa Clara Valley Water District)
industries.note: Title VIII creates a federal groundwater remediation fund administered with the district, reimbursing 65 percent of cleanup costs once a 35 percent non-federal match is deposited — a federal subsidy for a local water supplier serving ratepayers.
